newsitem.title: FRANCE: Air France says U.S. deals big cooperation step.
newsitem.headline: Air France says U.S. deals big cooperation step.

text.p: State-owned Air France said on Monday accords signed with two U.S. airlines, Delta Air Lines and Continental, have laid the basis for greater transatlantic co-operation -- vital to its ability to compete with its European rivals.
"It's a big step for Air France," said a spokeswoman. "This is the fruit of the letters of understanding signed on October 16."
The agreements were signed in the United States last Friday by Air France chairman Christian Blanc, the airline said.
The agreements followed a lengthy hunt by Air France for a U.S. partner, part of a strategy aimed at giving it a global reach and countering the spread of alliances among its rivals.
A key feature of the deals was agreement on code-sharing, a way to gain more customers without direct investment.

Passengers can be issued with a through ticket by one carrier to be used on its partner airline -- making it possible for airlines to supply passengers to each other without setting up their own routes.
Delta called the code-sharing agreement a catalyst for a "more positive aviation environment between the United States and France".
The agreements followed separate letters of intent signed by Air France last month with Delta and Continental, setting the stage for extensive co-operation in marketing and services.

The Air France spokeswoman said the aim of the agreements was to achieve closer linking of schedules and cooperation in the handling of passengers, freight, computer reservation systems and commercial sales and marketing programmes.
More than three million passengers travel between the United States and France every year in what is the third largest trans-Atlantic market.
The spokeswoman said Air France was still aiming to strike an alliance with an Asian carrier but said it was too early to say with which airline it might conclude a deal.

The airline, which has said it hopes to be in profit this financial year after posting a net loss of more than two billion francs last year due to big restructuring provisions, has said it hopes to find an Asian partner in 1997.
"We're proceeding step by step, first with North America and then Asia," she said.
